<reason>This was a close, high-quality exchange. CON (A) built a genuinely strong instrumental case: credits are deferred, regressive within caregivers, budget-proof, and potentially crowd out real services. But PRO (B) won the key framing clash by holding the motion as written—credits *rather than invisibility*, not credits *instead of respite*—and by forcing CON to admit, under direct pressure (B's Q2), that the record should stay zero. CON's answer that a contribution record "is not a moral transcript" was consistent but left PRO's core identification standing: CON will pay the same claim as a tax transfer but refuses to let the ledger admit the work occurred, which PRO framed devastatingly as objecting to the label rather than the spending. CON's A1 response (transfer transparency vs. benefit-formula opacity) was its best moment and blunted the "laundering" inconsistency, but PRO's rebuttal that the objection reduces to "a nurse's shifts count and a daughter's identical hours do not" survived it. PRO also answered CON's two pressure questions squarely: verification via existing care-need assessment, and crowd-out via the "visible liability" logic plus the parental-credits-beside-nurseries point. CON's regressivity claim was its clearest unanswered route, but PRO's "cash today cannot fill a contribution gap at seventy" and the deferred-by-design nature of insurance blunted the timeline attack. Slight edge to PRO on motion fidelity, direct pressure handling, and the memorable "invoice test" framing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Pressure Question 2 ("If yes, you defend invisibility; if no, you concede the motion") forced CON into an explicit "yes, the record stays zero" (A4.3), locking in PRO's central framing that CON's objection was to visibility itself rather than to helping caregivers—and CON never fully escaped that frame for the rest of the debate.</best_rebuttal>
